messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Adaeze is a 74-year-old African-born woman who has lived in a rural farming community in the American South for the better part of three decades. She works the land as she always has, tending crops with a steadiness that her neighbors have long admired. She lives with her long-term partner, a quiet man who has learned, over the past year, that there are distances inside Adaeze that he cannot seem to cross.

The assault occurred fourteen months ago, in the early morning hours when Adaeze had gone out alone to check on the irrigation lines at the edge of the property. It was still dark, the air thick with the smell of turned earth and damp soil, the kind of deep rural silence that had always felt, to her, like peace. A man she did not know attacked her among the rows. She was on the ground, her face pressed into the soil, the smell of it filling her mouth and nose throughout the assault. When it was over and he was gone, she lay in that same silence for a long time before she could move.

In the weeks that followed, Adaeze did not tell anyone what had happened. She returned to work because the land required it, but something had fundamentally shifted. The smell of freshly turned soil, which had once been inseparable from her sense of purpose and belonging, now arrived like a physical blow. Some mornings she would crouch beside a furrow and find herself back in the dark, unable to distinguish the present from that night. The anniversary of the assault, which she had marked privately and with dread in the months leading up to it, brought a week of barely functional days. And silence — the same deep rural quiet that had always accompanied her work — had become something she dreaded. When the wind died and the birds stopped and the world went still around her, her body responded as though the danger had never passed.

She had come to believe, in a way she could not fully articulate but felt with absolute certainty, that what happened had left something on her — not just a memory but a stain. She felt dirty in a way that washing did not reach, ashamed of her own body in a manner that made her avoid mirrors and recoil from her own reflection. Her partner, a gentle and patient man, had tried to hold her hand one evening and she had pulled away so sharply that she saw the hurt register on his face. She had not been able to explain it to him. Any form of touch, however tender, felt unbearable, and she had come to avoid it entirely, including the small physical gestures — a hand on the shoulder, an embrace — that had once been ordinary parts of her relationships.

To manage the days, Adaeze had developed a set of habits that she understood, on some level, were costing her. She forced herself to think only positive thoughts when the memories pressed close, repeating to herself that she was fortunate, that she was alive, that things could have been worse. She avoided working in the dark or at dusk, which had altered her schedule in ways that affected the farm's productivity and drawn questions from her partner and a neighbor who sometimes worked alongside her. She steered around anything that reminded her of that night — certain parts of the field, certain hours, certain weather. The life she had built around her work had quietly contracted.

What frightened her most, in the quietest part of herself, was a thought she had never spoken aloud: that she was no longer sure her life held the value it once had. She had survived many things, and she had always found her way back to the land and to herself. This time, she was not certain she could.

It was her partner who finally persuaded her to seek help, after she woke one night crying and would not let him near her. She came to the first session sitting very still, hands folded in her lap, and said that she had not told anyone the full story yet. What she hoped for, more than anything, was to be able to walk into her fields in the morning and smell the earth without it meaning what it now meant.
